Restored and annotated editions

The Willows

Algernon Blackwood

Blackwood, 1907. Two men camped on an island in the Danube, and a place that has noticed them. Nothing is ever shown, which is precisely the point.

Nothing happens, and it is unbearable.

Read more

Two men camp on a willow island in the Danube. The river rises. There are noises in the night. The island seems smaller in the morning. That is very nearly the whole of The Willows, and H. P. Lovecraft called it the finest weird tale in English without qualification.

Algernon Blackwood spent his twenties close to starving in New York and came out of it certain of one thing: that the natural world is not scenery. It is inhabited, it is aware, and it has no interest in us whatever. He is the ancestor of everything we now call folk horror.

Three stories, one argument made three times.

The Willows (1907), a sandbank in the Danube and something that has no name and no shape

Ancient Sorceries (1908), a small French town where the people are unhurried, watchful and curiously feline, and a mild Englishman who gets off the train for no reason he can explain

The Wendigo (1910), the Canadian bush, and a voice that comes back from far overhead

This annotated edition adds:

An original introduction placing Blackwood between the Victorian ghost story and the cosmic horror that followed him

A headnote before every story

A glossary of the places, peoples and beliefs the stories depend on

H. P. Lovecraft on Blackwood, whom he called the one absolute and unquestioned master of weird atmosphere

We had strayed into some region where the risks were great, yet unintelligible to us.

What this edition adds

  • The Willows with Ancient Sorceries and The Wendigo
  • An Introduction, plus a dated headnote for each story
  • A glossary of Blackwood's world
  • Lovecraft's essay on Blackwood, reprinted
